body:
Examples of SEO titles for service pages and articles: 30 templates. The title that appears in blue in Google results decides, within seconds, whether a visitor clicks on your page or on the competitor's below it.

Below you will find thirty examples of SEO titles ready to adapt, split by page type, each with its real length in characters. You can copy them and replace only the business name, the city or the product.

Examples of SEO titles for service pages and articles: 30 templates

An SEO title, technically called a title tag, is the text that appears in the browser tab and as the link on the Google results page. It is not the same as the H1 heading visible on the page, although the two can partly overlap.

Google usually displays the first 50 to 60 characters of a title, with the rest cut off by an ellipsis. That is why each example below has its exact length noted next to it, not an estimate.

What makes an SEO title effective

A good title does two things at once: it tells Google what the page is about and it shows the reader why this particular result is worth opening, rather than the one above or below it. The formulas below take both into account.

  • The main keyword close to the start of the title, not buried at the end.
  • A length under 60 characters, so it is not cut off on the results page.
  • A differentiating element: the city, the year, the client type or a concrete benefit.
  • Clarity above all, with no ambiguous wording or exaggerated promises.
  • Every page has a unique title; two pages with identical titles compete over the same intent.

These rules apply the same way to a service page as to the SEO optimization page of your own site or to a blog article. Only the formulas differ, depending on the page type.

The criteria above do not work in isolation. A title with the keyword at the start but no differentiating element gets lost among ten other results with an identical structure. Conversely, an original title without the keyword somewhere in plain sight does not help the page get found by the search engine, however good it sounds to a human reader. That is why each example below combines a clear keyword with a concrete detail: a city, a year, a client type or a real figure about delivery or about the content of the page.

Examples of titles for service pages

Service pages compete on commercial keywords, where the search intent is clear: someone wants to hire someone. The title must immediately say what service you offer and for whom. This is not the place for vague wording such as "complete solutions" or "trusted partners", which say nothing about the actual service and contain no word anyone would search for.

Titles for local and portfolio pages

  1. SEO optimization Cluj-Napoca: consulting for local businesses (61 characters)
  2. Technical SEO for online stores: audit and implementation (57 characters)
  3. Local SEO for practices and clinics: visibility guide (53 characters)
  4. National SEO consulting: expansion into new markets (51 characters)
  5. SEO portfolio: completed projects, verifiable results (53 characters)

When the page targets a single city or area, the city goes directly into the title, not just into the page text. For client networks spread across several cities, the formula stays the same, only the city changes from one page to another, with no other changes to the structure.

Titles for pricing pages and related services

  1. SEO optimization price: transparent packages for 2026 (53 characters)
  2. Professional SEO services for companies in Romania (50 characters)
  3. White Hat link building: safe strategies for authority (54 characters)
  4. Social media marketing for local brands (39 characters)
  5. Shopify SEO: optimization for international stores (50 characters)

The pricing page deserves a title separate from the service page, because the search intent is different: someone searching for the price has already decided they want the service, they just want to know what it costs. A title that speaks directly about packages and transparency answers exactly that.

Examples of titles for blog articles

Informational articles compete on a different intent: someone is looking for an answer, not an offer. Titles that start with "how", "examples of" or "template for" describe exactly what the reader gets inside.

Step-by-step guide titles

  1. How to write an effective SEO title in five steps (49 characters)
  2. Complete guide to optimizing page titles (40 characters)
  3. How to check the length of a title before publishing (52 characters)
  4. How to choose the right keyword for the title (45 characters)
  5. Practical guide to article titles that bring clicks (51 characters)

List-style titles with examples

  1. Examples of titles for list-type articles (41 characters)
  2. Examples of titles for step-by-step guides (42 characters)
  3. Title template for comparison articles (38 characters)
  4. Examples of titles for articles about Google (44 characters)
  5. Title template for internal case studies (40 characters)

The "examples of" formula works best when the article really contains the examples themselves, numbered and ready to copy, not just general advice on how to write them yourself. A reader looking for a template wants to leave with something concrete in hand.

Examples of titles for online store pages

Category and product pages in an online store need short titles, with the product name first and a detail that matters to the buyer: size, season or delivery time.

Titles for category pages

  1. Women's dresses: the 2026 summer collection (43 characters)
  2. Men's sports footwear: fast delivery in Romania (47 characters)
  3. Living room furniture: complete sets at manufacturer prices (59 characters)
  4. Natural cosmetics: daily skin care (34 characters)
  5. Educational toys for kids: recommended from age 3 (49 characters)

Titles for product pages

  1. Original auto parts: delivery within 24 hours (45 characters)
  2. Electronics and accessories: extended warranty included (55 characters)
  3. Children's books: the autumn-winter 2026 collection (51 characters)
  4. Sports equipment: for the gym and outdoors (42 characters)
  5. Flowers and floral arrangements: same-day delivery (50 characters)

For a store with thousands of products, identical titles from one page to the next are the most common problem. A title field generated automatically from the product name, with a single variable detail added manually, solves the problem without repetitive work on every page.

Common mistakes that ruin a good title

Many weak titles are not wrong from the start, but become weak because they repeat the same habits across dozens of pages. The most common ones are easy to recognize and to fix.

Identical titles are the most common of them, especially on sites with many category or product pages. When Google meets dozens of identical titles, it does not know which page to show for a search and picks one itself, sometimes a different one from the one you would have chosen. The result is that well-written pages stay hidden, not because they are weak, but because their title does not set them apart from their neighbors.

  • Identical titles on different pages, for example "Home" repeated across the multi-language versions of the site.
  • The keyword repeated several times in the same title, which looks artificial to the reader.
  • Titles written entirely in capitals, which attract attention on the results page for the wrong reasons.
  • No city or area on a clearly local page, even though the page competes on exactly that keyword.
  • Promises the page cannot back up, such as a guaranteed position in Google.

The last mistake deserves a separate mention: a title that promises a guaranteed result attracts the click, but loses trust the second the reader lands on the technical SEO page and finds no such guarantee.

How to check the length of a title before publishing

The number of characters is a clue, but Google actually cuts the title by its width in pixels, not by a fixed number of letters. Wide letters such as "m" or "w" take up more space than "i" or "l", so two titles with the same number of characters can display differently.

In practice, a letter like "m" takes up about twice the width of a letter like "i", so a title full of wide letters gets cut earlier than one with thin letters, even if both have exactly 58 characters. The character count is still a useful benchmark, because it is quicker to calculate than the pixel width and in most cases leads to the same practical result.

The practical check takes three steps, with no complicated tools.

  • Write the title in a plain text editor and count the characters, as a quick benchmark under 60.
  • Search for the proposed title in Google, in a private window, to see exactly where the display is cut.
  • Choose the exact keyword before writing the title, not after, with the help of a keyword generator, so you do not rewrite the title from scratch.

For pages that also display structured data, for example reviews or frequently asked questions, also check that the title stays correct after Google adds rich snippets, using a structured data validator. The details of implementing the right schema are described in the guide to structured data. A good title combined with correct structured data takes up more visual space on the results page.

The thirty examples above are starting formulas, not texts to copy word for word. Adapt them to your own service or product, check the real length and keep a unique title for each page. For a full audit of the titles already on your site, alongside the other technical signals, use technical SEO or start from SEO optimization. If you often write product or category pages, URL structure matters as much as the title, as explained in URL structure and its impact on rankings. And if your articles also need ready-to-copy examples for other sections of the site, such as customer reviews, the templates in examples of good reviews follow the same principle as the titles above: concrete, verifiable and short.
